steps.label: Browser Checks Cache
steps.description: Before asking anyone else, the browser looks up the hostname in its own DNS cache. If it already has a recent answer, it uses that IP address immediately without making any network requests.

steps.label: OS & Hosts File Check
steps.description: If the browser cache misses, the operating system checks its own DNS cache and the local hosts file. This is where entries like 127.0.0.1 localhost are defined and always resolved first.

steps.label: Query Recursive Resolver
steps.description: The OS sends a DNS query to a recursive resolver — usually provided by your ISP or a public service like 8.8.8.8. This resolver does the heavy lifting of finding the answer on your behalf.

steps.label: Root Name Server
steps.description: If the resolver doesn't have the answer cached, it asks a root name server. There are 13 sets of root servers worldwide. They don't know the IP, but they know which TLD server to ask next.

steps.label: TLD Name Server
steps.description: The resolver asks the TLD name server for the domain's extension (e.g. .com, .org). The TLD server responds with the address of the authoritative name server for the specific domain.

steps.label: Authoritative Name Server
steps.description: The resolver queries the authoritative name server — the definitive source of DNS records for this domain. It returns the A record containing the actual IP address of the server.

steps.label: IP Address Returned
steps.description: The recursive resolver caches the answer and returns the IP address to the operating system, which passes it to the browser. The browser can now open a TCP connection to that IP.
